```{r setup}
library(multisiteDGP)
```

A simulated data set never matches its design exactly, and the diagnostics
say how far apart the two are. This vignette explains the four blocks that
`summary()` prints and what the `pass`, `warn`, and `fail` statuses beside
some rows do and do not say. It then shows how `scenario_audit()` checks a
grid of designs over many simulated data sets, and lists the nine presets
with the source of their values.

## What `summary()` reports

```{r summary}
dat <- sim_multisite(preset_education_modest(), seed = 1)
summary(dat)
```

A row holds the realized value, then the target when the design sets one,
then a status when a rule applies to the row. Six of the values have a
function of their own, which takes the simulated data and returns the number
in the summary to more digits.

```{r functions}
c(informativeness(dat), heterogeneity_ratio(dat), realized_rank_corr(dat))
c(ks_distance(dat), bhattacharyya_coef(dat), mean_shrinkage(dat))
```

### Scale

The `sigma_tau` row is the standard deviation of the 50 simulated site
effects, 0.166 against 0.200 in the design. The geometric mean of the
sampling variances `se2_j` (0.092) stands for the sampling variance of a
typical site. `informativeness()` combines it with the `sigma_tau` of the
design into $I = \sigma_\tau^2 / (\sigma_\tau^2 + \mathrm{GM}(se_j^2))$. $I$
lies between 0 and 1 and is larger when the estimates say more about the site
effects. `heterogeneity_ratio()` returns $R$, the largest sampling variance
divided by the smallest. $I$ and $R$ have no target here, because
`sim_multisite()` derives the standard errors from site sizes. With
`sim_meta()` the design sets both, and the rows show a target and a status.

### Dependence

`realized_rank_corr()` returns the Spearman correlation between the
standardized site effects `z_j` and the sampling variances `se2_j`. A
positive value means that sites with larger effects tend to be less precise.
The design has no dependence between effects and precision, so the target is
0, and 0.254 is what 50 independent pairs happened to produce. The marginal
row uses `tau_j` in place of `z_j` and differs from the residual row only
when the design has covariates. The two Pearson rows are descriptive, with no
target and no status. `vignette("effect-precision-dependence")` covers
designs that ask for a correlation.

### Shape

The shape block compares the 50 values of `z_j` with the distribution in the
design, here the standard normal. `ks_distance()` returns the
Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, the largest gap between the empirical
distribution function of the `z_j` and the normal distribution function. The
`p` beside it is the p-value of the test. `bhattacharyya_coef()` returns the
overlap, between 0 and 1, of the histogram of the `z_j` and the histogram of
50 normal quantiles at evenly spaced probabilities, both on the same 50 bins.
The Q-Q residual is the largest absolute difference between the sorted `z_j`
and those quantiles. The block is printed only when `true_dist` is
`"Gaussian"` or `"StudentT"`. For another distribution, give either function
two numeric vectors, `z_j` and a large sample from the distribution.

### Precision

The precision block describes how precisely single sites can be estimated. The
shrinkage of site $j$ is $S_j = \sigma_\tau^2 / (\sigma_\tau^2 + se_j^2)$, the
weight of the site's own estimate in its posterior mean when effects and
estimates are normal. For other effect distributions it is not an exact
weight. `mean_shrinkage()` returns the average of the $S_j$. The average
margin of error (0.617) is 1.96 times the average standard error, the
half-width of a 95 percent interval for a typical site. Both rows use the
standard errors and the `sigma_tau` of the design.

### Statuses

Five rows carry a status. The rules are stored with the diagnostics, and
the column `warn_rule` gives the values that earn a `warn`. Values on the
better side of that range pass and values on the worse side fail.

```{r rules}
tab <- attr(dat, "diagnostics")$target_vs_realized
tab[!is.na(tab$status), c("diagnostic", "status", "warn_rule")]
```

In these rules `realized` is the value in the summary, `delta` is its
difference from the target, and `J` is the number of sites. The first three
rules compare one data set with its design and allow for the sampling error
of `J` sites. `SE` in the `sigma_tau` rule is the standard error of the
standard deviation of `J` draws,
$\sigma_\tau \sqrt{(k - 1 + 2 / (J - 1)) / (4 J)}$ for a distribution with
kurtosis $k$. For the normal distribution ($k = 3$) it is
$\sigma_\tau / \sqrt{2 (J - 1)}$, here 0.020, so 0.166 is 1.7 standard errors
below 0.200 and the row passes. The rule for the rank correlation uses 2 and
3 times $1 / \sqrt{J - 1}$, the standard error of a rank correlation between
independent variables. The KS distance is judged by its p-value. The
Bhattacharyya coefficient has no status, because its size depends on the
number of sites more than on the fit, and the Q-Q residual has no rule. The
next example simulates 400 data sets and counts the statuses.

```{r seeds}
statuses <- function(seed) {
  d <- sim_multisite(preset_education_modest(), seed = seed)
  tab <- attr(d, "diagnostics")$target_vs_realized
  tab[!is.na(tab$status), c("diagnostic", "status")]
}
runs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:400, statuses))
runs$status <- factor(runs$status, levels = c("pass", "warn", "fail"))
table(runs)
```

Three statuses compare one draw with the design and change with the seed. The
`sigma_tau` row passes in 383 of the 400 data sets, the rank correlation in
376, and the KS distance in 386. Each of these rules passes a data set
simulated from its design about 95 times in 100, so a `warn` on one row is
expected in about 1 data set in 20. The `sigma_tau` row passes less often when
a few sites carry most of the variance, as in a mixture with a rare and
distant component (70 times in 100 with `eps = 0.05`, `delta = 50`, 25 sites).

The other two statuses describe the design. Mean shrinkage passes in all 400
data sets, and the average margin of error warns in all 400, because it is
more than twice `sigma_tau`. Such a status changes with the seed only when
the design is close to the boundary of its rule.

## Thresholds

`scenario_audit()` checks a design over many simulated data sets and uses
three thresholds of its own, which `default_thresholds()` returns.

```{r thresholds}
str(default_thresholds())
```

`mean_shrinkage_min` is a lower threshold for mean shrinkage and `R_max` an
upper threshold for the heterogeneity ratio $R$. `ks_scaled_max` is an upper
threshold for the KS distance times $\sqrt{J}$. When the site effects come
from the distribution of the design, that product has nearly the same
distribution for any number of sites, with a median near 0.8, and it exceeds
1.63 in about 1 data set in 100. A design fails if the median of a diagnostic
over its data sets is on the wrong side of a threshold. It gets a `warn` if
every median is within the thresholds but the 5th percentile of mean shrinkage
is below its threshold, or the 95th percentile of $R$ or of the KS distance is
above its threshold. These thresholds belong to `scenario_audit()` only. The
rules behind the statuses of `summary()` are fixed, and `scenario_audit()`
asks for a mean shrinkage of 0.30 where `summary()` passes 0.10. To change a
threshold, give `scenario_audit()` a named list as `thresholds`.

## When a diagnostic fails

A `warn` or a `fail` in the precision block has one of two causes. With small
site sizes, the standard errors are large relative to `sigma_tau`, mean
shrinkage is low, and the margin of error is wide. A larger `nj_mean` or a
larger `R2` reduces the standard errors. The other cause is a small
`sigma_tau`. `preset_education_small()` sets `sigma_tau = 0.05` with site
sizes that average 40, and both precision rows fail in every data set. If
that is the trial to be simulated, the statuses describe it and the design
can stay.

In the other blocks a single `warn` is usually chance, and a `fail` is rare:
the table above has one among 1,200 statuses. A `warn` or a `fail` in many
data sets from one design has one of two causes. The simulated values do not
follow the design, as when `hybrid_polish = "none"` leaves a rank correlation
away from its target. Or the rule does not fit the design, as for the
`sigma_tau` row of such a mixture.

## Checking a grid of designs

`design_grid()` crosses the values given for design arguments and returns one
design for each combination. `base_design` supplies the arguments that do not
vary, and `seed_root`, which is required, gives every design its own seed.

```{r grid}
grid <- design_grid(
  J = c(50, 200), nj_mean = c(25, 100),
  base_design = preset_education_modest(), seed_root = 1
)
grid
```

`scenario_audit()` simulates each row of the grid, which it calls a scenario,
`M` times (200 by default), starting from the seed in the row. It then
summarizes the diagnostics over the data sets.

```{r audit}
audit <- scenario_audit(grid, M = 50)
audit
audit$fail_reasons
audit[, c("J", "nj_mean", "med_mean_shrinkage", "med_ks")]
```

The two designs with an average site size of 100 pass, with 50 sites and
with 200. `groups_evaluated` lists the blocks behind a status. Dependence is
never among them, and shape only for a design with a shape block. Each entry
of `fail_reasons` names a diagnostic, the statistic that was compared, and
the threshold, and `warn_reasons` has the same form. The two designs with
`nj_mean = 25` fail on mean shrinkage, whose median is 0.193 whatever the
number of sites. The median KS distance is 0.114 and 0.115 with 50 sites and
about half that with 200. Its threshold moves in the same way: 1.63 divided
by $\sqrt{J}$ is 0.231 with 50 sites and 0.115 with 200. A study that accepts
less shrinkage can lower the threshold for mean shrinkage.

```{r audit-own}
own <- list(mean_shrinkage_min = 0.15)
scenario_audit(grid[1, ], M = 50, thresholds = own)$status
```

The design in row 1 now passes.

## The presets

Seven presets derive the standard errors from site sizes and are simulated
with `sim_multisite()`. Two set them directly from $I$ and $R$ and are
simulated with `sim_meta()`. All nine have grand mean `tau = 0` and no
dependence between effects and precision.

| Preset | Sites | Distribution | `sigma_tau` | Standard errors | Source of the values |
|----------------------------|-----|---------|-------|----------------------|------------------------------|
| `preset_education_small()` | 50 | Gaussian | 0.05 | from site sizes, `nj_mean = 40` | `sigma_tau` from published estimates [@weiss2017howmuch], rest assumed |
| `preset_education_modest()` | 50 | Gaussian | 0.20 | from site sizes, `nj_mean = 50` | `sigma_tau` from published estimates [@weiss2017howmuch], rest assumed |
| `preset_education_substantial()` | 100 | Gaussian | 0.30 | from site sizes, `nj_mean = 80` | `sigma_tau` from published estimates [@weiss2017howmuch], rest assumed |
| `preset_jebs_paper()` | 50 | Mixture | 0.20 | from site sizes, `nj_mean = 40` | published simulation design [@lee2025improving] |
| `preset_jebs_strict()` | 100 | Mixture | 0.15 | from site sizes, `nj_mean = 80` | published simulation design [@lee2025improving] |
| `preset_walters_2024()` | 46 | Gaussian | 0.197 | from site sizes, `nj_mean = 240` | `J` and `sigma_tau` published [@walters2024empirical], rest assumed |
| `preset_twin_towers()` | 1000 | Mixture | 2 | from site sizes, all 100 | assumed |
| `preset_meta_modest()` | 50 | Gaussian | 0.20 | set directly, `I = 0.3`, `R = 1.5` | assumed |
| `preset_small_area_estimation()` | 30 | Gaussian | 0.20 | set directly, `I = 0.2`, `R = 3` | assumed |

Weiss et al. [-@weiss2017howmuch] report cross-site standard deviations for 16
multisite trials of education and training programs. The education presets
take `sigma_tau` from the small end, the middle, and the upper end of that
range. Two presets are named after Lee et al. [-@lee2025improving], published
in the Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics (JEBS). Both are cells
of that paper's simulation grid, with its mixture and its site-size generator
(`engine = "censored"`). For a seed, each returns the numbers of the paper's
code once the sites are sorted by size, as that code sorts them.
`preset_walters_2024()` also takes an average sampling variance of 0.010 from
its source: a site of the average size, 240, has that variance under the
assumed `R2 = 0.4`. The last three presets have no source.
`preset_twin_towers()` has two well separated components and is meant for
methods that recover the shape of the effect distribution.
`preset_small_area_estimation()` has a wider spread of precision than
`preset_meta_modest()`, as small-area estimates do.

## Overriding a preset

A preset passes its arguments to `multisitedgp_design()`, so any argument of
that function replaces the value in the preset, as `vignette("multisiteDGP")`
shows. The example gives `preset_education_substantial()` the 50 sites of
`preset_education_small()` and plots each estimate against its site effect.

```{r compare, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Estimates follow the site effects (dashed line of equality) in the right panel and are unrelated to them in the left panel."}
library(ggplot2)
small <- sim_multisite(preset_education_small(), seed = 1)
large <- sim_multisite(preset_education_substantial(J = 50), seed = 1)
c(informativeness(small), informativeness(large))
both <- rbind(data.frame(preset = "small", small),
              data.frame(preset = "substantial", large))
ggplot(both, aes(tau_j, tau_j_hat)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~preset)
```

In the left panel the site effects lie within about 0.1 of zero and the
estimates range from about $-0.7$ to 0.6, so an estimate says almost nothing
about its site. Informativeness is 0.021 for that design and 0.608 for the
one on the right.
